# Glossary {#sec-glossary}

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen_book.py from glossary.yml. Do not edit; add terms to glossary.yml. -->

The words this book uses with a fixed meaning. Each entry links to the section that introduces it.

## 2 {.unnumbered}

2D prefix sum
:   P[r][c] = the sum of the rectangle above and left of (r, c). Any rectangle sum is four lookups by inclusion–exclusion. See @sec-pref-2d.

## 3 {.unnumbered}

3SUM conjecture
:   The unproved assumption that 3SUM (three numbers summing to zero) has no O(n^(2−ε)) algorithm; many quadratic lower bounds are conditional on it. See @sec-tp-fix.

## A {.unnumbered}

Adaptive sort
:   A sort that runs faster on input that is already partly sorted, such as insertion sort (O(n + inversions)) or Timsort (O(n) on sorted input). See @sec-salgo-a0.

Adjacency list
:   A graph stored as, for every vertex, the list of its neighbours. Uses O(V + E) memory and lists the neighbours of a vertex in time proportional to its degree. See @sec-gr-store.

Alignment
:   A way to line up two strings with gaps; each alignment is a monotone path in the grid of their prefixes, so edit distance and LCS are shortest/longest paths. See @sec-st-align.

Amortized cost
:   The average cost per operation over any sequence of operations, as opposed to the worst cost of a single one. A dynamic array's append is O(1) amortized even though one append can copy everything. See @sec-cx-amortized.

Anti-diagonal
:   The cells with a constant value of i + j. Main diagonals have constant i − j; both make good grouping keys. See @sec-mat-a2.

Anti-hash test
:   An input built so that many keys collide in a particular hash table implementation, turning expected O(1) lookups into O(n). Defeated by a randomised hash. See @sec-hash-anti.

Antichain
:   A set of elements no two of which are comparable. Dilworth's theorem: the fewest chains covering a poset equals its largest antichain. See @sec-lis-chain.

At-most difference
:   Counting windows with exactly k of something as atMost(k) − atMost(k − 1), because "exactly k" is not shrink-safe but "at most k" is. See @sec-sw-a4.

Automaton DP
:   A DP whose state includes the state of an automaton reading a pattern (KMP or a trie), used to count or build strings that avoid or contain a pattern. See @sec-st-auto.

## B {.unnumbered}

Back edge
:   In a DFS, an edge to an ancestor that is still on the stack (grey). A directed graph has a cycle exactly when its DFS finds a back edge. See @sec-df-tree.

Backtracking
:   DFS over partial solutions: extend the current choice, recurse, then undo it. Pruning cuts branches that cannot lead to an answer. See @sec-df-p4.

Big-O
:   f = O(g) means f grows no faster than a constant times g for large inputs. It is an upper bound, not an exact count. See @sec-cx-notation.

Binary search on the answer
:   Binary-searching a range of candidate answers instead of an array, using a monotone feasibility test (for example "can we ship within D days at capacity c?"). See @sec-bst-a5.

Block-swap rotation
:   Rotating an array by repeatedly swapping equal-length blocks; it does exactly n − gcd(n, k) swaps. See @sec-part-rotate-blockswap.

Boyer–Moore voting
:   A one-pass, O(1)-memory way to find the element that appears more than n/2 times, by pairing off different values. See @sec-hash-vote.

Bucket sort
:   Scatter the values into equal-width buckets, sort each bucket, and concatenate; expected O(n) when the input is uniformly distributed. See @sec-lts-a4.

## C {.unnumbered}

Cache line
:   The fixed-size block (typically 64 bytes) in which memory moves between RAM and the CPU cache. Scanning an array in order uses every byte of each line it loads. See @sec-arr-cache.

Canonical key
:   A normal form that equal-up-to-symmetry objects share (a sorted word for anagrams, a reduced fraction for a slope), so grouping becomes a hash-map lookup. See @sec-hash-keys.

Checkerboard colouring
:   Colouring cell (i, j) by (i + j) mod 2. Every move to a side neighbour flips the colour, which gives parity arguments about paths and tilings. See @sec-mat-a6.

Complement lookup
:   Looking up the partner value (for example t − x) in a map of the elements seen so far, so each pair is found in one pass. See @sec-hash-complement.

Complementary counting
:   Counting the objects with a property by counting all objects and subtracting those without it. See @sec-cnt-comp.

Contribution technique
:   Computing a sum over many objects (subarrays, pairs) by swapping the order of summation: add up each element's value times the number of objects it belongs to. See @sec-cnt-a1.

Coordinate compression
:   Replacing values by their rank among the sorted distinct values, so huge or negative values can index an array of size n. See @sec-srt-a4.

Counter of counters
:   A table indexed by frequency that records how many keys (or which keys) have each count, so "maximum frequency" or "how many keys appear exactly k times" is O(1). See @sec-ds-a3.

Counting sort
:   Sorting integer keys in [0, k) by counting each key, taking prefix sums to get each key's first position, and placing the records stably; O(n + k). See @sec-lts-a1.

Cover count
:   The number of subarrays of an n-element array that contain index i: (i + 1)(n − i). See @sec-cnt-a1.

Cycle decomposition
:   Splitting a permutation into disjoint loops i → p[i] → p[p[i]] → … that return to their start. See @sec-idx-a4.

Cyclic sort
:   Swapping each value to its home index until every position holds its own value. On a permutation it uses exactly n − c swaps (c cycles), the minimum. See @sec-idx-a2.

## D {.unnumbered}

Decision tree (sorting)
:   A binary tree of comparisons whose leaves are the possible output orders. It has at least n! leaves, so its height, the worst-case number of comparisons, is Ω(n log n). See @sec-lts-a1-wall.

Degree
:   The number of edges at a vertex (in-degree and out-degree in a directed graph). The degrees sum to twice the number of edges. See @sec-gr-p1.

DFS tree
:   The tree formed by the edges a depth-first search follows to discover new vertices. Every other edge is a back, forward or cross edge relative to it. See @sec-df-tree.

Difference array
:   The array of differences d[i] = a[i] − a[i−1]. Adding v to a whole range of a becomes two point updates on d; a prefix sum turns d back into a. See @sec-pref-diff.

Dynamic programming
:   Solving a problem by naming subproblems (states), writing how each one follows from smaller ones (transitions), and computing each state once. See @sec-dpi-what.

## E {.unnumbered}

Edit distance
:   The fewest insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one string into another. A path in the prefix grid of the two strings. See @sec-st-p2.

Entry and exit times
:   The moments a DFS first reaches a vertex and finishes it. u is an ancestor of v exactly when u's interval contains v's. See @sec-df-time.

Event sweep
:   A sparse difference array: store the +v and −v changes at range ends in a map, sort the positions, and sweep a running total. It replaces a difference array when coordinates are huge. See @sec-pref-diff.

Exchange argument
:   A proof that a greedy choice is safe: take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one and swap parts of it toward the greedy choice without making it worse. See @sec-pf-greedy.

## F {.unnumbered}

First-index map
:   A hash map from a prefix value to the earliest index where it occurs, used to find the longest subarray with a given sum. See @sec-pref-hash.

Fix-two-rows reduction
:   Fixing a top and a bottom row and collapsing the band between them into column sums, so a 2D rectangle problem becomes a 1D array problem. See @sec-mat-a5.

Flood fill
:   Marking every cell connected to a start cell in a grid by DFS or BFS: a grid is a graph whose edges are the neighbouring cells. See @sec-gr-p3.

Frequency array
:   An array indexed by value that counts occurrences; it replaces a hash map when the values are small integers (after an offset for negatives). See @sec-arr-p5.

Functional graph
:   A directed graph in which every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge. Every walk eventually enters a cycle (a "rho" shape). See @sec-gr-p5.

## G {.unnumbered}

Gap method
:   Merging two sorted arrays in place with O(1) extra space by comparing positions a shrinking gap apart, as in Shell sort. See @sec-tp-merge.

Group pointer
:   A second index that jumps over a maximal run of equal (or related) elements, so that one piece of work settles the whole block. See @sec-tp-runs.

## H {.unnumbered}

Half-open range
:   The range [l, r) that includes l and excludes r. Its length is r − l and two adjacent ranges [a, b) and [b, c) share no element, which removes most off-by-one errors. See @sec-arr-ranges.

Harmonic sum
:   n/1 + n/2 + … + n/n = O(n log n): the cost of looping over the multiples of every number up to n. See @sec-cx-p2.

## I {.unnumbered}

Implicit graph
:   A graph that is never stored: its vertices are states (a number, a board, a string) and its edges are the legal moves, generated on the fly. See @sec-gr-p4.

Inclusion–exclusion
:   |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|, and its generalisation with alternating signs over all intersections. See @sec-cnt-comp.

Index-compatible array
:   An array of length n whose values all lie in 1..n (or 0..n−1), so every value names a valid index and the array can mark or sort itself in place. See @sec-idx-a1.

Interactive problem
:   A problem where the program asks a judge questions and reads its answers. Flush after every query and test against a local judge. See @sec-test-interactive.

Interval partitioning
:   Assigning intervals to the fewest rooms so that no room holds two overlapping intervals; the fewest rooms equals the peak overlap. See @sec-int-events.

Introsort
:   Quicksort with a recursion-depth limit that switches to heapsort when exceeded and finishes small ranges with insertion sort; O(n log n) worst case. It is how std::sort is usually implemented. See @sec-salgo-a7.

Invariant
:   A statement that is true before a loop starts and stays true after every iteration. At the end it, together with the exit condition, gives the result. See @sec-pf-invariants.

Inversion
:   A pair of positions i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Insertion sort does exactly one swap per inversion, and merge sort can count them in O(n log n). See @sec-salgo-a0.

## K {.unnumbered}

Kadane's algorithm
:   The O(n) maximum-subarray scan that keeps the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index. See @sec-dpi-p5.

## L {.unnumbered}

Lazy reset
:   Replacing a global clear with a version clock: bump the clock, and treat any cell whose stamp is older than the clock as empty. See @sec-ds-a5.

Lehmer code
:   The rank of a permutation in lexicographic order, written digit by digit as the number of smaller unused values at each position. See @sec-part-rank.

Level-order traversal
:   Visiting a tree level by level with a queue. One round of the queue (its size at the start of the round) is exactly one level. See @sec-tv-level.

Load factor
:   n/m, the average number of keys per bucket of a hash table. Tables resize when it passes a threshold, which keeps lookups expected O(1). See @sec-hash-sets.

Longest common subsequence
:   The longest sequence that appears, in order but not necessarily contiguously, in both of two strings. Computed on the grid of their prefixes. See @sec-st-p1.

Longest increasing subsequence
:   The longest strictly increasing subsequence of an array. O(n²) by DP over the last element, O(n log n) with the tails array and binary search. See @sec-lis-p1.

Loop invariant
:   See Invariant. See @sec-pf-invariants.

lower_bound and upper_bound
:   lower_bound (Python bisect_left) is the first index with a[i] ≥ x; upper_bound (bisect_right) is the first index with a[i] > x. Their difference counts the copies of x. See @sec-bst-a2.

LSD radix sort
:   One stable counting sort per digit, least significant digit first; Θ(d(n + b)) for d digits in base b. Stability is what keeps earlier passes' order. See @sec-lts-a3.

## M {.unnumbered}

Master theorem
:   The solution of T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), found by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a): the leaves dominate, the levels balance (an extra log n), or the root dominates. See @sec-cx-recurrences.

Memoisation
:   Top-down DP: a recursive function that stores each result the first time it is computed and returns the stored value afterwards. See @sec-dpi-styles.

Misra–Gries
:   The generalisation of Boyer–Moore voting: k counters find every value that occurs more than n/(k+1) times, followed by one verification pass. See @sec-hash-vote.

Monotone predicate
:   A yes/no test whose answers over an ordered set run false … false, true … true. Binary search finds the boundary in O(log n) tests. See @sec-bst-a1.

Monotonic deque
:   A deque whose values stay sorted, used to keep the minimum or maximum of a sliding window in O(1) amortized per step. See @sec-od-fast.

Monovariant
:   A quantity that only moves in one direction as a process runs. If it is bounded, the process must stop. See @sec-pf-process.

Morris traversal
:   An inorder traversal with O(1) extra memory that temporarily threads the tree through right pointers of predecessors, then restores it. See @sec-tv-morris.

MSD radix sort
:   A counting sort on the leading digit or character, then recursion into each group; it suits strings of different lengths. See @sec-lts-a3-msd.

## N {.unnumbered}

Next permutation
:   The smallest permutation larger than the current one in lexicographic order: find the last ascent, swap with the smallest larger value to its right, reverse the suffix. See @sec-part-perm.

## O {.unnumbered}

Order of a permutation
:   The smallest k > 0 with p^k equal to the identity; it is the least common multiple of the cycle lengths. See @sec-idx-a6.

## P {.unnumbered}

Parent array
:   A rooted tree stored as parent[v] for every vertex (−1 for the root). Enough to walk up, and to compute subtree values in reverse BFS order. See @sec-tr-p4.

Parity of a permutation
:   The parity of n − c, which equals the parity of every sequence of swaps that sorts the permutation. See @sec-idx-a4.

Partition DP
:   A DP over where the last block of a cut starts: dp[i] = best over j of dp[j] + cost(j, i). The block [j, i) is half-open. See @sec-od-part.

Perfect shuffle
:   Interleaving the two halves of an array (a1 b1 a2 b2 …); doing it in place in O(n) time needs the cycle-leader method. See @sec-part-shuffle.

Pigeonhole principle
:   If more than n items go into n boxes, some box holds two. Used to prove that a repeat, a cycle or a collision must exist. See @sec-pf-contradiction.

Prefix count
:   Prefix sums of a 0/1 indicator array, so the number of cells with a property in [l, r) is P[r] − P[l]. See @sec-pref-def.

Prefix sum
:   The array P with P[i] = a[0] + … + a[i−1]. Any range sum becomes P[r] − P[l] in O(1). See @sec-pref-def.

Pull and push
:   Two directions for the same DP. Pull computes dp[i] from cells already final; push stands at i and writes into every cell it reaches. Same dependency graph, different loop. See @sec-od-dir.

## Q {.unnumbered}

Quickselect
:   Partition around a pivot, then keep only the side that holds the target rank; expected O(n) to find the k-th smallest element. See @sec-salgo-a4-select.

## R {.unnumbered}

Read/write pointers
:   Compacting an array in place: a read index scans every element and a write index marks where the next kept element goes. See @sec-arr-p2.

Recurrence
:   An equation that gives the cost (or the value) on an input of size n from its values on smaller inputs, such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. See @sec-cx-recurrences.

Recurrence relation (DP)
:   See Transition. See @sec-dpi-recipe.

Rolling array
:   Keeping only the rows of a DP table that the next row reads, so a 2D table costs O(width) memory. See @sec-gd-mem.

Rooting a tree
:   Choosing a root in an edge list and orienting every edge away from it by one DFS or BFS, which gives parents, depths and subtrees. See @sec-tr-p6.

Rotation orbit
:   The up-to-four cells that a quarter turn of a square matrix cycles through; rotating in place moves each orbit with one 4-cycle. See @sec-mat-a3.

Row-major order
:   Storing a matrix row after row, so cell (i, j) of an R×C grid sits at index i·C + j. Walking along a row reads memory in order. See @sec-mat-a1.

## S {.unnumbered}

Scatter and gather
:   Writing each element to the position it names (scatter, out[p[i]] = a[i]) versus reading from the position named (gather, out[i] = a[p[i]]); they apply a permutation and its inverse. See @sec-idx-a6.

Sentinel
:   An extra element placed at a boundary so that the boundary behaves like any other position, removing a special case from the loop. See @sec-arr-sentinel.

Separate chaining and open addressing
:   The two ways to store colliding keys: a list per bucket (chaining), or probing other slots of the same array (open addressing). See @sec-hash-sets.

Serialisation
:   Writing a tree as a string, including markers for missing children, so that it can be rebuilt exactly. Equal subtrees then get equal strings or ids. See @sec-tv-ser.

Shrink-safe rule
:   A window condition such that every sub-window of a valid window is also valid. It is what lets the left end move only forward, giving O(n) in total. See @sec-sw-a2.

Shrinking
:   Reducing a failing random test to the smallest input that still fails, by deleting or simplifying parts while the bug persists. See @sec-test-shrinking.

Sliding window
:   A contiguous range a[l..r] kept up to date as it moves, by adding the entering element and removing the leaving one instead of recomputing. See @sec-sw-a1.

Sparse set
:   The Briggs–Torczon pair of arrays (dense list plus sparse index) that supports insert, delete, membership and clear in O(1), even on uninitialised memory. See @sec-ds-a5-sparse.

Spiral order
:   Reading a grid by walking its outer ring and then moving the four walls inward, ring by ring. See @sec-mat-a2.

Stabbing set
:   The fewest points such that every interval contains at least one. Greedy: sort by right end, and place a point at each uncovered interval's right end. See @sec-int-sched.

Stable partition
:   A partition that keeps the original relative order inside each block. Easy with O(n) extra space; in place it costs O(n log n) with rotations. See @sec-part-stable.

Stable rearrangement
:   A rearrangement in which elements the rule does not distinguish keep their relative order (a stable sort, or compacting with read/write pointers). See @sec-arr-inplace.

Stable sort
:   A sort in which elements with equal keys keep their input order, so sorting by one key and then stably by another sorts by both. See @sec-srt-a1.

State
:   In DP, the smallest description of a subproblem that still determines its answer, such as "the best result for the first i items". See @sec-dpi-recipe.

Stress test
:   Running a fast solution and a brute force on many small random inputs and stopping at the first disagreement. See @sec-test-stress.

Strict weak ordering
:   A "comes before" rule that is irreflexive and transitive, with transitive ties. It is what std::sort requires of a comparator; `<=` breaks it. See @sec-srt-a2.

Subtree aggregation
:   Computing a value for every subtree (size, sum, height) in post-order: a vertex's value combines its children's values. See @sec-df-p2.

Swap-with-last deletion
:   Deleting from an unordered packed array in O(1) by moving the last element into the hole and popping; an index map is updated for the moved element. See @sec-ds-a1.

Sweep line
:   Turning intervals into sorted +1/−1 events and processing them left to right with a running count, so overlap questions cost O(n log n). See @sec-int-events.

## T {.unnumbered}

Tabulation
:   Bottom-up DP: filling the table in an order in which every state's dependencies are already computed. See @sec-dpi-styles.

Tails array
:   In the O(n log n) LIS, tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. It stays sorted, so each element is placed by binary search. See @sec-lis-p1.

Three-way partition
:   Rearranging an array into three blocks (less than, equal to, greater than a pivot) in one pass with three pointers; also called the Dutch national flag problem. See @sec-part-dnf.

Timsort
:   A stable, adaptive merge sort that finds natural runs, extends short ones with binary insertion sort, and merges runs under a stack invariant; Python's sorted uses it. See @sec-salgo-a8.

Tombstone
:   A marker left in a deleted open-addressing slot so that probe sequences passing through it still find keys stored further along. See @sec-ds-a4.

Topological order
:   An order of the vertices of a DAG in which every edge goes forward. A DP's states must be computed in such an order of its dependency graph. See @sec-df-box.

Transition
:   In DP, the formula that gives a state from smaller states, usually found by asking "what was the last decision?". See @sec-dpi-recipe.

Transpose
:   Reflecting a matrix across its main diagonal, A[i][j] = M[j][i]. Transpose followed by reversing each row rotates a square matrix 90° clockwise. See @sec-mat-a3.

Tree
:   A connected graph with no cycle; equivalently, n vertices and n − 1 edges and connected. There is exactly one path between any two vertices. See @sec-tr-what.

Two pointers
:   Two indices that only move forward (or toward each other), so the scan costs O(n) in total even though it considers pairs. See @sec-tp-inv.

## V {.unnumbered}

Virtual index
:   A remapping of positions (for example 1, 3, 5, …, 0, 2, 4, …) under which an ordinary partition places values into a wiggle order in place. See @sec-part-virtual.

## W {.unnumbered}

Weighted interval scheduling
:   Pick non-overlapping intervals of maximum total weight. Sort by end; dp[i] = max(skip i, take i plus the best ending before i starts). See @sec-od-p2.

Weighted median
:   The first value, in sorted order, whose cumulative weight reaches half the total. It minimises the sum of w_i |x_i − t|. See @sec-srt-p5-b.
